title: What exactly is it about Herzog’s work?

commenti.body: I think his best documentary is *Into the Abyss*. It’s surprisingly different for Herzog, it’s about a white trash death row inmate in Texas. He stays away from the sensationalism of the crime but instead focuses on the people involved; victims, law enforcement, prison workers and the perpetrator himself. The narrative and message shifts into a very Herzog-esque message that we all have complex lives and emotions and that there’s joy and sorrow in this world.

I can't remember if I read it or if I thought (was into him 20+ years ago) it but his documentaries are typically stylised fiction, or at least play very loose with the truth and his fictional films are more real than anyone else's. Documentaries almost. Fitzcarraldo being the standout obviously but this applies to nearly everything. Who else would really bother to drag a boat over a hill in the Amazon jungle? Without any effects.

Thematically, there are a bunch of things he's obsessed with. Stylistically, I don't think he's as coherent as a lot of auteurs. He just does what he feels like and suits the material. Cares more about getting the idea on film than how and sticking to a style.

I love his stuff because he has a different take than any other documentarian/filmmaker and lets his voice come through with commentary. The movies he makes are more like a dialogue with the subject matter and him expressing how making the movie changed him in the process. I also like that he is so well spoken but also so full of rage/passion at times, it makes him stand out with his own unique voice. And lastly, I think he is one of the few filmmakers than can choose to leave some mysteries undisturbed because of his own personal feelings. He doesn’t feel like he needs to play for us the recording of Timothy treadwells death for instance. We get enough out of seeing him experience it, and are left wanting more but being denied. His stuff just stands out as unique for me ya know?

>I’m especially curious about his visual style and techniques. Though it generally seems rather subtle, there is something that *feels* distinctive, but I can’t seem to put into words.

>Thematically, I know he often explores the indifference of nature and the “ecstatic truth.”

To me, one theme (perhaps *the theme*) running throughout Herzog's filmography (both fiction and documentary) is that of obsessed people embarking on an incredible personal quest, sometimes futile, that cuts them off from their relationships and from society. Aguirre searching for El Dorado, Fitzcarraldo transporting a steamboat across the Amazon, Timothy Treadwell leaving the human world to live with bears, Walter Steiner pursuing the world ski jumping record, Graham Dorrington building his own airship and flying it across Guyana, scientists leaving friends and family and community to live and work in Antarctica.

To me, the constant return to that theme (probably autobiographical) is a defining aspect of Herzog's filmography. And not just his filmography -- his novel *Das Dämmern der Welt*, about a Japanese soldier on a remote island who continues to fight World War II long after Japan's surrender, is very much in this vein.

>Stylistically, I don't think he's as coherent as a lot of auteurs. He just does what he feels like and suits the material. Cares more about getting the idea on film than how and sticking to a style.

To me, that's a good thing, a strength. I like that he doesn't have a little bag of tricks that he keeps pulling out for every movie.

A lot of the best auteurs are like that. 

Friedkin is similar I'd say. More about the material than replicating previous work and becoming a self parody. I love Wes Anderson but he falls into this.

For me what unites Herzog’s body of work is a quest for what he calls “the ecstatic truth” whether it’s via documentary or fiction, or in his usual manner a blend of both.

I’d say his most important documentaries visually are “Fata Morgana” and “Lessons of Darkness” because of the hallucinatory quality of the landscapes and the images he makes of them.

They’re also never without humor, which is part of his appeal and what makes Herzog a little different from other auteurs who make immersive meditative cinema. Stuff like the monkey at the end of “Aguirre.” Or the unexpected deadpan joke about the oil firefighters in “Lessons of Darkness.”

I always say that he goes to the edges of humanity and films the people he meets there - whether it's Antarctica or meteors destroying earth or volcanoes or death row or death by grizzly bear or early cave paintings or aborigines or the jungles of the Amazon - anywhere that's at the edge of civilization or confronting the end of life. 

His filmmaking approach is as a documentarian, even when it's a narrative film, and he's fine with blurring the lines between documentary and fiction, but the aesthetics are secondary to the people he's filming (although there's more care to storytelling in his 70s and 80s films than anything lately).
Ron Howard is also diving into the documentary realm lately.

That's true but he doesn't really have the cultural cachet of a Herzog or a Scorsese. And certainly doesn't have a *Last Waltz* or *Grizzly Man* or *Land of Silence and Darkness*-level classic in his filmography yet.

thank you! do you have any observations about his visual style?
Would suggest the multiple books of Herzog interviews for insights into his style.

As for visual technique, he's very fond of telephoto zoom shots with a lot of parallax motion. Look at the way he captures the ski jumping in Great Ecstasy of Woodcarver Steiner, or the helicopter shots circling Kinski in Aguirre and Fitzcarraldo - always keeping the subject still in the center while the environment churns around them. I think that's a key visual motif for him. He also likes to apply slo-mo (Woyzeck, Heart of Glass) or even to approximate the effect (Nosferatu). 

I think The Mountain is a central motif across both his fiction and documentary work, and in a way he's the greatest Bergfilm director.
[removed]

He's the kind of guy who's game to go anywhere, somewhere exotic or unusual, with just a backpack and a few essential needs (like Butterfingers candy bars). He'll come back with his journal and pictures of all the oddities he's found. He's passionate and likes to observe people who are the same way. He's funny, sometimes inadvertently; there's something pretentious about his work and the way he talks about it as though it were profound statements of the universe. Sometimes his visual style and content is like someone who's taken drugs. He'll be remembered, if at all, not as a visionary, but an oddity.
I saw that one. Great stuff as usual

I love the guy, but I don't get his narrative films at all. They are just a mess and lack any coherent style except that of shooting from the hip. That works much better in his documentaries than in his narrative films. Not a great stance from a cinephile, and I'm sure the downvotes will be coming, but it's how I feel.

This one is free on YouTube. It's depressing as shit, though, like right from the open moment where a pastor describes what It's like to give people on death row their last rites. You can tell he feels for these people, and it always makes me sad.

For his style, one thing I can notice is he is not afraid to "set a scene" in the sense that because everything he does is real, he can take a long time scanning over things. I love this, I find for me, it helps me follow along or get into these stories because the places honestly just feel real. Scenes in "Rescue Dawn" don't feel like they are inside a Vietnam movie, it just feels like they are in Vietnam. I tried to explain that the best I could, but I can't quite place the words to do it. I hope that makes sense.
You don't think *Aguirre* is visionary filmmaking?
Some nice cinematography, but the story's clunky and is there really much to say about it?

[J. Hoberman:](https://web.archive.org/web/20070306012142/http://www.villagevoice.com/film/0642%2Choberman%2C74738%2C20.html)

>The premise is scary. The tone is absurd. The mood, cued by the lush drone of Popol Vuh's score, is languorous, even trippy. The drama ends in a fever of denial—someone hallucinates a boat in a tree, someone else dies from a nonexistent arrow. Alone with corpses and monkeys on a raft that drifts in circles as it is circled by the camera, Aguirre is the last man standing—ranting still, amid the illusion of brute existence.

>History repeats itself in the jungle. Ending with mass suicide in deepest Guyana, the story of Jim Jones and his Peoples Temple is both the death rattle of '60s utopianism and—predicated on the desire to found a New Jerusalem in the wilderness—a very American saga.

>...

>We can only imagine the cult leader's Aguirre moment—the late afternoon he lorded over a kingdom of corpses.

Francis Ford Coppola:

>Aguirre, with its incredible imagery, was a very strong influence.

Victoria Stiles:

>Unlike the historical Aguirre, this one has unusually large features and is beardless and blond. Through this blond Nordic knight, Herzog alludes to a much earlier age of expansionism: to medieval Germany with the religious imperialism of the Crusaders and the Teutonic Knights, and also to a more recent period: the 1930s, which combined the rebirth of the Nordic stereotype (seen in the light of racial superiority) with Hitler's attempts at imperialist conquest. Herzog's main character is more than a conquistador of one particular century; he is the embodiment of imperialism as such.

Philip French:

>First released in 1972, it brought together for the first time two of the wildest, most explosive talents in world cinema, Herzog himself and Klaus Kinski, who plays Aguirre, a paranoid, power-crazed Spanish conquistador. Magnificently shot by Thomas Mauch under appalling conditions, it begins and ends with stunning images. The first is a breathtaking five-minute sequence of a vast procession of soldiers, priests and well-dressed ladies winding up and down a precipitous Peruvian valley. The second, a metaphor for a civilisation gone mad or a colonial impulse gone lunatically astray, focuses on the crazed Aguirre strutting around a drifting raft with no one to listen to his grandiose ravings except the hundreds of monkeys that chatter around him.
Pretentious.

You asked if there's anything to say about the film besides the cinematography. I responded with a few passages from people with a lot to say about its historical and sociopolitical subtext. You might find their interpretations pretentious, but I think I've demonstrated that there is a lot to say about *Aguirre, the Wrath of God*.
What do you mean when you say his films lack a coherent style?

>He'll be remembered, if at all, not as a visionary or great filmmaker, but as an oddity.

A counterexample: no fewer than 13 Werner Herzog-directed films got votes in the 2022 BFI/*Sight and Sound* poll. 

*Aguirre, The Wrath of God* finished tied for 128th place.

*Fitzcarraldo* tied for 314th. Three more films in the top 1,000.
I don’t know how else to put that. If you randomly showed two of his movies to someone without credits they’d likely not know it was the same director.

I'm not sure that's necessarily a bad thing. To me, it points to a certain range and willingness to take on new creative challenges. 

You wouldn't drag Martin Scorsese because some random person might not assume that *Mean Streets* and *Hugo* were directed by the same person.
You are comparing the extremes within directors’ works. And even in those examples there is more in common than any two of Herzog’s you want to pick.

Kubrick directed so many types of movies (horror, sci-fi, heist, pastoral coming of age, etc.) that while he has signatures that run throughout, he mostly adapted his style to fit the film.


I love Wes Anderson, but he is the extremest opposite.

But why is a consistent style necessarily better than range? Not every filmmaker needs to be Wes Anderson. And, as I mentioned in another comment above, a single thematic thread runs throughout his entire filmography. From a writing/choice of subject matter perspective, his filmography (fiction and nonfiction) is very coherent.
I range is fine. Again, I find no coherent style. I think o he shoots from the hip and whatever sticks, sticks.
It's crazy how Herzog describes Michael Perry as one of the the most dangerous persons he has ever met. For Herzog to say that about you, you must be something special. Phenomenal documentary.

I think you are spot on. Lessons from Darkness has a somewhat more poetic theme like the one you describe, as in the monumental event that was the lighting of the fires and the incredible effort to put them down.
People say the same thing about Kubrick. It really isn’t a bad thing.
That one I’ve never heard. I just don’t like his movies. You two are welcome to still enjoy them.

>there's something pretentious about his work and the way he talks about it as though it were profound statements of the universe

I dunno I don't agree. His narrations are remarkably profound to me. I think it's because he has a naturally surreal and descriptive way of talking. His films are in a way so successful because they're about crazy big premises, but he handles them with such care and grace. None of his films presume to condescend about their subjects. It would be so easy to dismiss Timothy Treadwell in Grizzly Man for example as a lone nutter in the wilderness, and indeed some of the park rangers do, but Herzog conveys such empathy and understanding in trying to work out exactly what drew Timothy to the bears.
Good points — his documentary filmmaking reflects a radical empathy that is the polar opposite of pretension.
Pretentious is almost always an adjective that says more about the person who uses it than about what they describe.

I think you can see differences in style if you look into which cinematographers he worked with, he was / is very loyal to his cinematographers and most of his films where shot by one of by three people, Mauch, Schmidt-Reitwein and Zeitlinger, a few by Klausmann, but I think the first three names are the most important in his oeuvre and there are stylistic differences between the Mauch, Schmidt-Reitwein and (especially) Zeitlinger phases.
Lessons of Darkness is such a haunting film.  It feels so intensely human and alien at the same time.

Madness seems like the through line in a lot of his work. The man couldn’t make a documentary segment about penguins without making it about madness. I’d like to clarify that this is as far from a complaint as possible
I’m not sure a man who watched Wreslemania and Honey Boo Boo can really be pretentious
That’s a good observation regarding the environment around the character

In The White Diamond, he even abandons the main guy building his airship for a while to focus on yet another outsider, who is friends with his rooster. Like character documentary inception.

As far as I can tell, this happens in every single documentary, for example in Cave of Forgotten Dreams there is the cave-sniffer and during the interview with the young french researcher he makes a point of including the part where the guy talks about the time he worked in a circus.

Where the Green Ants Dream is a bit fiction and a bit documentary.

Herzog is fond of the idea that environments have personalities. A hallmark of his mode of storytelling is the use of animals in particular settings to convey emotion. Rats in a boat in Nosferatu, bears in Grizzly Man, Amazonian monkeys in Aguirre. Small figures in huge imposing landscapes that seem to have their own personalities is a running motif for him.

One of my all time favorite films and a very good anti-death penalty movie. Crucially, there are two murderers and only one of them got the death penalty, mostly because his accomplice had character witnesses who were able to garner sympathy with the jury.
